claim: Apicomplexan parasites cause persistent mortality and morbidity worldwide through diseases including malaria, toxoplasmosis, and cryptosporidiosis.
source: Apicomplexan parasites cause persistent mortality and morbidity worldwide through diseases including malaria, toxoplasmosis, and cryptosporidiosis (Havelaar et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Havelaar et al., 2015

claim: Toxoplasma gondii infects more than 2 billion people.
source: The phylum member Toxoplasma gondii alone infects >2 billion people.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about T. gondii infection prevalence

claim: Ca2+ signals and their downstream effectors impact almost every cellular function in apicomplexans.
source: Ca2+ signals and their downstream effectors are a part of the signaling cascade that impacts almost every cellular function (Lourido and Moreno, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lourido and Moreno, 2015

claim: Ca2+ signaling in apicomplexans results in diverse downstream events central to parasite virulence, including secretion of adhesive proteins, motility, and invasion into and egress from host cells.
source: Signaling begins with release of Ca2+ from intracellular stores or influx through plasma membrane channels, resulting in diverse downstream events central to parasite virulence, including secretion of adhesive proteins, motility, and invasion into and egress from host cells.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about Ca2+ signaling functions

claim: Signal-transducing components downstream of Ca2+ release are largely unknown in apicomplexans.
source: Signal-transducing components downstream of Ca2+ release are largely unknown yet are likely essential for apicomplexan viability and virulence (Lourido and Moreno, 2015; Nagamune and Sibley, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lourido and Moreno, 2015 and Nagamune and Sibley, 2006

claim: Genomic searches for canonical Ca2+-binding domains in apicomplexans have identified several individual proteins involved in transducing and effectuating Ca2+ signals.
source: Genomic searches for canonical Ca2+-binding domains in apicomplexans have identified several individual proteins involved in transducing and effectuating Ca2+ signals (Farrell et al., 2012; Huet et al., 2018; McCoy et al., 2017), like kinases, phosphatases, and transporters (Hortua Triana et al., 2018; Lourido et al., 2012; Lourido et al., 2010; Luo et al., 2005; Márquez-Nogueras et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Many key signaling elements involved in fundamental Ca2+ responses are either missing from apicomplexan genomes or have diverged beyond recognition.
source: However, many of the key signaling elements involved in fundamental Ca2+ responses—including the channels responsible for its stimulated release—are either missing from apicomplexan genomes or have diverged beyond recognition, suggesting that eukaryotic pathogens evolved novel pathways for Ca2+ mobilization and transduction (Billker et al., 2009; Lourido and Moreno, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Billker et al., 2009 and Lourido and Moreno, 2015

claim: Ca2+-dependent protein kinases (CDPKs) are the only known Ca2+-regulated kinases in the apicomplexan phylum.
source: In apicomplexans, Ca2+-dependent protein kinases (CDPKs) have garnered the most attention as the only known Ca2+-regulated kinases in the phylum (Billker et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Billker et al., 2009

claim: CDPKs possess intrinsic Ca2+-binding sites and do not rely on CaM like mammalian CaMKs.
source: These kinases possess intrinsic Ca2+-binding sites and do not rely on CaM-like mammalian CaMKs.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about CDPK structure

claim: Several CDPKs in T. gondii trigger parasite motility.
source: In T. gondii, several of these CDPKs trigger parasite motility (Lourido et al., 2012; Lourido et al., 2010; McCoy et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2022; Treeck et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: TgCDPK7 plays a role in replication.
source: The roles of TgCDPK7 in replication and TgCDPK2 in amylopectin granule formation also implicate Ca2+ signaling in cellular functions outside the kinetic phase of the parasite lytic cycle (Morlon-Guyot et al., 2014; Bansal et al., 2021; Uboldi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Morlon-Guyot et al., 2014; Bansal et al., 2021; Uboldi et al., 2015

claim: TgCDPK2 plays a role in amylopectin granule formation.
source: The roles of TgCDPK7 in replication and TgCDPK2 in amylopectin granule formation also implicate Ca2+ signaling in cellular functions outside the kinetic phase of the parasite lytic cycle (Morlon-Guyot et al., 2014; Bansal et al., 2021; Uboldi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Morlon-Guyot et al., 2014; Bansal et al., 2021; Uboldi et al., 2015

claim: Dephosphorylation has garnered comparatively little attention in apicomplexan parasites.
source: Dephosphorylation has garnered comparatively little attention in these parasites (Yang and Arrizabalaga, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang and Arrizabalaga, 2017

claim: The client proteins of CaM and calcineurin remain largely unknown in apicomplexans.
source: The roles of the prototypical CaM and the Ca2+/CaM-dependent phosphatase calcineurin have only been phenotypically examined, and their client proteins remain largely unknown (Paul et al., 2015; Philip and Waters, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Paul et al., 2015 and Philip and Waters, 2015

claim: No systematic efforts have been undertaken to globally map the Ca2+ signaling pathways of apicomplexan parasites.
source: Although key players are conserved and essential across the Apicomplexa, no systematic efforts have been undertaken to globally map the Ca2+ signaling pathways of these pathogens.
evidence: Statement about the state of the field prior to this study

claim: The study mapped the Ca2+-responsive proteome of T. gondii via time-resolved phosphoproteomics and thermal proteome profiling.
source: We mapped the Ca2+-responsive proteome of the model apicomplexan Taxoplasma gondii via time-resolved phosphoproteomics and thermal proteome profiling.
evidence: Description of the experimental approach used in the study

claim: The waves of phosphoregulation following PKG activation and stimulated Ca2+ release corroborate known physiological changes.
source: The waves of phosphoregulation following PKG activation and stimulated Ca2+ release corroborate known physiological changes but identify specific proteins operating in these pathways.
evidence: Summary of findings from the phosphoproteomics experiments

claim: Thermal profiling of parasite extracts identified many expected Ca2+-responsive proteins, such as parasite Ca2+-dependent protein kinases.
source: Thermal profiling of parasite extracts identified many expected Ca2+-responsive proteins, such as parasite Ca2+-dependent protein kinases.
evidence: Summary of findings from thermal profiling experiments

claim: The study identified numerous Ca2+-responsive proteins that are not predicted to bind Ca2+, yet are critical components of the parasite signaling network.
source: Our approach also identified numerous Ca2+-responsive proteins that are not predicted to bind Ca2+, yet are critical components of the parasite signaling network.
evidence: Summary of findings from the study

claim: Protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) is a Ca2+-responsive enzyme that relocalized to the parasite apex upon Ca2+ store release.
source: We characterized protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) as a Ca2+-responsive enzyme that relocalized to the parasite apex upon Ca2+ store release.
evidence: Summary of findings about PP1 from the study

claim: Conditional depletion of PP1 revealed that the phosphatase regulates Ca2+ uptake to promote parasite motility.
source: Conditional depletion of PP1 revealed that the phosphatase regulates Ca2+ uptake to promote parasite motility.
evidence: Summary of findings from PP1 depletion experiments

claim: PP1 may be partly responsible for Ca2+-regulated serine/threonine phosphatase activity in apicomplexan parasites.
source: PP1 may thus be partly responsible for Ca2+-regulated serine/threonine phosphatase activity in apicomplexan parasites.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of PP1 findings

claim: Zaprinast stimulates PKG activation by inhibiting phosphodiesterases that degrade cGMP.
source: We can emulate the endogenous signaling pathways that mediate the kinetic phase of the lytic cycle by treating isolated parasites with zaprinast, which stimulates PKG activation by inhibiting phosphodiesterases that degrade cGMP (Brown et al., 2016; Lourido et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brown et al., 2016 and Lourido et al., 2012

claim: Zaprinast-stimulated motility occurs rapidly and in defined sequence in apicomplexans.
source: Zaprinast-stimulated motility occurs rapidly and in defined sequence in apicomplexans: initially, an increase in cGMP activates parasite protein kinase G (PKG), which phosphorylates substrates and stimulates Ca2+ release from internal stores (Brown et al., 2020; Lourido and Moreno, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brown et al., 2020 and Lourido and Moreno, 2015

claim: PKG likely performs functions that extend beyond regulating Ca2+ stores.
source: PKG likely performs functions that extend beyond regulating Ca2+ stores, for example by mobilizing diacylglycerol and phosphatidic acid (Lourido et al., 2012; Brown et al., 2017; Bullen et al., 2016; Bisio et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: TgCDPK1 and TgCDPK3 synergize with PKG to effectuate microneme secretion and parasite motility.
source: Ca2+-dependent protein kinases, such as TgCDPK1 and TgCDPK3, synergize with PKG to effectuate microneme secretion and parasite motility (Brown et al., 2016; Lourido et al., 2012; Lourido et al., 2010; McCoy et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The cGMP/Ca2+ signaling cascade is active within seconds of cGMP elevation.
source: This signaling cascade is active within seconds of cGMP elevation
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about signaling kinetics

claim: Existing T. gondii phosphoproteomes compare changes at a single time point following Ca2+-ionophore stimulation.
source: however, existing T. gondii phosphoproteomes compare changes at a single time point following Ca2+-ionophore stimulation (Treeck et al., 2014), providing only a snapshot of diverging signaling states.
evidence: Supported by citation to Treeck et al., 2014

claim: The study quantified dynamic changes in the phosphoproteome within a minute of stimulation with zaprinast.
source: We quantified dynamic changes in the phosphoproteome within a minute of stimulation with zaprinast and thus activation of the cGMP/Ca2+ pathway.
evidence: Description of the experimental approach

claim: The study collected five timepoints in the 60 s following stimulation (0, 5, 10, 30, and 60 s), as well as three DMSO-treated matched timepoints (0, 10, and 30 s), in biological duplicate.
source: We collected five timepoints in the 60 s following stimulation (0, 5, 10, 30, and 60 s), as well as three DMSO-treated matched timepoints (0, 10, and 30 s), in biological duplicate (Figure 1A).
evidence: Description of experimental design with reference to Figure 1A

claim: The study used TMTpro labeling methods to multiplex 16 samples.
source: Using TMTpro labeling methods (Li et al., 2020), we multiplexed 16 samples, allowing us to analyze a complete time course, with replicates and controls, in a single MS experiment.
evidence: Description of experimental method with citation to Li et al., 2020

claim: Phosphopeptides were enriched using sequential metal-oxide affinity chromatography.
source: Phosphopeptides were enriched from the rest of the sample using sequential metal-oxide affinity chromatography, which maximizes phosphopeptide capture (Tsai et al., 2014).
evidence: Description of experimental method with citation to Tsai et al., 2014

claim: The experiments quantified 4,055 parasite proteins.
source: Our experiments quantified 4,055 parasite proteins, none of which exhibited more than a twofold change in abundance in the 60 s following stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Data from the experiments with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: None of the quantified proteins exhibited more than a twofold change in abundance in the 60 s following stimulation.
source: Our experiments quantified 4,055 parasite proteins, none of which exhibited more than a twofold change in abundance in the 60 s following stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Data from the experiments with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The study quantified 11,755 unique phosphopeptides belonging to 2,690 phosphoproteins.
source: From a phosphoproteome of 11,755 unique peptides with quantification values (belonging to 2,690 phosphoproteins), 839 phosphopeptides increased in abundance three modified Z scores above the median, whereas 154 decreased 1.8 Z scores below the median.
evidence: Data from the phosphoproteomics experiments

claim: 839 phosphopeptides increased in abundance three modified Z scores above the median.
source: From a phosphoproteome of 11,755 unique peptides with quantification values (belonging to 2,690 phosphoproteins), 839 phosphopeptides increased in abundance three modified Z scores above the median, whereas 154 decreased 1.8 Z scores below the median.
evidence: Data from the phosphoproteomics experiments

claim: 154 phosphopeptides decreased 1.8 Z scores below the median.
source: From a phosphoproteome of 11,755 unique peptides with quantification values (belonging to 2,690 phosphoproteins), 839 phosphopeptides increased in abundance three modified Z scores above the median, whereas 154 decreased 1.8 Z scores below the median.
evidence: Data from the phosphoproteomics experiments

claim: Principal component analysis on the significant peptides distinguished the agonist treatment and time-course kinetics in the two principal components accounting for the greatest variability in the data.
source: Principal component analysis on the significant peptides distinguished the agonist treatment and time-course kinetics in the two principal components accounting for the greatest variability in the data (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Data analysis results with reference to figures

claim: A Gaussian mixture-model clustering algorithm heuristically resolved four clusters for phosphopeptides arising from zaprinast treatment.
source: A Gaussian mixture-model clustering algorithm (Invergo et al., 2017) heuristically resolved four clusters for phosphopeptides arising from zaprinast treatment: three clusters increasing with different kinetics, and one decreasing (Figure 1D).
evidence: Data analysis results with citation to Invergo et al., 2017 and reference to Figure 1D

claim: Cluster 1 contains 173 phosphopeptides that increased sharply in abundance within 5 s of treatment and continued to increase for the remainder of the time course.
source: On average, the 173 phosphopeptides belonging to cluster 1 increased sharply in abundance within 5 s of treatment and continued to increase for the remainder of the time course (Figure 1D), suggesting that they belonged to the first wave of phosphoregulation.
evidence: Data from clustering analysis with reference to Figure 1D

claim: Cluster 1 was enriched for phosphoproteins associated with phosphodiesterase activity, phospholipid binding, and Ca2+ binding.
source: This cluster was enriched for phosphoproteins associated with phosphodiesterase activity, phospholipid binding, and Ca2+ binding (Figure 1E), including PDE1, PDE2, PI4,5K, PI3,4K, PI-PLC, a phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-triphosphate 5-phosphatase, a putative Sec14, TgCDPK2A and TgCDPK7, and PPM2B (Table 1 and Figure 1F).
evidence: Data from enrichment analysis with references to figures and table

claim: Cluster 2 contains 173 phosphopeptides that increased more gradually and exhibited lower fold-changes than cluster 1 sites.
source: Peptides in clusters 2 and 3 (173 and 527, respectively) increased more gradually and exhibited lower fold-changes than cluster 1 sites (Figure 1D).
evidence: Data from clustering analysis with reference to Figure 1D

claim: Cluster 2 was enriched in proteins functioning in transport of monovalent ions and lipids, cyclase activity, and Ca2+ binding.
source: Cluster 2 was notably enriched in proteins functioning in transport of monovalent ions and lipids, cyclase activity, and Ca2+ binding (Figure 1E).
evidence: Data from enrichment analysis with reference to Figure 1E

claim: Cluster 3 contains 527 phosphopeptides.
source: Peptides in clusters 2 and 3 (173 and 527, respectively) increased more gradually and exhibited lower fold-changes than cluster 1 sites (Figure 1D).
evidence: Data from clustering analysis with reference to Figure 1D

claim: Cluster 3 is enriched for phosphoproteins with metal transporter activity.
source: Clusters 2 and 3 are enriched for phosphoproteins with metal transporter activity, including ATPases such as TgA1, the putative copper transporter CuTP, a putative P5B-ATPase, a putative E1-E2 ATPase, and TgATP4.
evidence: Data from enrichment analysis

claim: Small-molecule transporters are phosphorylated at later time points in the zaprinast response.
source: As observed in other T. gondii Ca2+-stimulated phosphoproteomes, at later time points small-molecule transporters are phosphorylated, including MFS transporters, ApiAT5-3, and TgFNT2.
evidence: Data from the study compared to other phosphoproteomes

claim: The guanylyl and adenylyl cyclases are extensively modified during the zaprinast response.
source: The guanylyl and adenylyl cyclases are also extensively modified, as are the cyclase organizers UGO and AIP.
evidence: Data from the phosphoproteomics experiments

claim: Cluster 3 is uniquely enriched in proteins functioning in subcellular remodeling, vesicle trafficking, and glideosome activity.
source: Cluster 3, which represents a latter wave of phosphoregulation, is uniquely enriched in proteins functioning in subcellular remodeling, vesicle trafficking, and glideosome activity (Figure 1E).
evidence: Data from enrichment analysis with reference to Figure 1E

claim: Cluster 4 is the only cluster characterized by decreasing phosphorylation.
source: Cluster 4, the only cluster characterized by decreasing phosphorylation, was functionally enriched in phosphoproteins involved in transporter and MAP kinase activity.
evidence: Data from clustering and enrichment analysis

claim: ERK7 was dephosphorylated within 30 s of zaprinast treatment.
source: ERK7 was dephosphorylated within 30 s of zaprinast treatment, whereas TgTLK2 was dephosphorylated only at the final 60 s time point.
evidence: Data from the phosphoproteomics experiments

claim: TgTLK2 was dephosphorylated only at the final 60 s time point.
source: ERK7 was dephosphorylated within 30 s of zaprinast treatment, whereas TgTLK2 was dephosphorylated only at the final 60 s time point.
evidence: Data from the phosphoproteomics experiments

claim: ERK7 regulates conoid and cytoskeletal stability during cell division, with secondary functions in parasite egress, motility, and invasion.
source: ERK7 regulates conoid and cytoskeletal stability during cell division, with secondary functions in parasite egress, motility, and invasion (Back et al., 2020; Dos Santos Pacheco et al., 2021; O'Shaughnessy et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: TLK2 regulates parasite replication.
source: TLK2 regulates parasite replication (Smith et al., 2022; Varberg et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al., 2022 and Varberg et al., 2018

claim: Cluster 4 was the only class of peptides that was not functionally enriched in Ca2+ binding proteins.
source: Cluster 4 was the only class of peptides that was not functionally enriched in Ca2+ binding proteins (Figure 1E).
evidence: Data from enrichment analysis with reference to Figure 1E

claim: SCE1 is a TgCDPK3 target.
source: Indeed, SCE1 was implied to be a TgCDPK3 target through a genetic suppressor screen (McCoy et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to McCoy et al., 2017

claim: TGGT1_309910 is the ortholog of Plasmodium falciparum Pf ICM1, a PKG substrate.
source: TGGT1_309910 is the ortholog of Plasmodium falciparum Pf ICM1, a PKG substrate identified through proteomic interaction studies (Balestra et al., 2021), although it remains uncharacterized in T. gondii.
evidence: Supported by citation to Balestra et al., 2021

claim: The guanylyl cyclase, PDE2, and a Ca2+ influx channel with EF hands exhibit peptides belonging to both increasing and decreasing clusters.
source: Along with the guanylyl cyclase, the cAMP-specific phosphodiesterase PDE2 and a Ca2+ influx channel with EF hands exhibit peptides belonging to both increasing and decreasing clusters.
evidence: Data from the phosphoproteomics experiments

claim: The phosphoproteome identifies candidate mediators of the feedback between cyclic-nucleotide and Ca2+ signaling.
source: Our phosphoproteome thus identifies candidate mediators of the feedback between cyclic-nucleotide and Ca2+ signaling.
evidence: Interpretation of the phosphoproteomics data

claim: The first cluster likely includes the most proximal targets of PKG.
source: The first cluster likely includes the most proximal targets of PKG.
evidence: Inference from the kinetics of phosphorylation

claim: PI-PLC is a substrate of PKG in P. falciparum.
source: Previous PKG-dependent phosphoproteomes from the related apicomplexan P. falciparum similarly implicate PI-PLC as a substrate of the kinase (Alam et al., 2015; Balestra et al., 2021; Brochet et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The product of PI-PLC activity, IP3, stimulates Ca2+ store release in parasites.
source: The product of PI-PLC activity, IP3, stimulates Ca2+ store release in parasites (Garcia et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Garcia et al., 2017

claim: Phosphoproteins in clusters 2, 3 and 4 likely contain the targets of Ca2+-regulated kinases and phosphatases.
source: In turn, phosphoproteins in clusters 2, 3 and 4 likely contain the targets of Ca2+-regulated kinases and phosphatases.
evidence: Inference from the kinetics of phosphorylation

claim: Thermal proteome profiling (TPP) has been used to identify small molecule–target interactions in living cells and cell extracts.
source: Thermal proteome profiling (TPP) has been used to identify small molecule–target interactions in living cells and cell extracts (Dai et al., 2019; Mateus et al., 2020; Savitski et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: TPP operates on the premise that ligand binding induces a thermal stability shift.
source: TPP operates on the premise that ligand binding induces a thermal stability shift, stabilizing, or destabilizing proteins that change conformationally in response to the ligand, and such changes in stability can be quantified by MS (Dziekan et al., 2020; Reinhard et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dziekan et al., 2020 and Reinhard et al., 2015

claim: The authors previously used TPP to identify the target of the antiparasitic compound ENH1.
source: We previously used this method to identify the target of the antiparasitic compound ENH1 (Herneisen et al., 2020; Herneisen and Lourido, 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to Herneisen et al., 2020 and Herneisen and Lourido, 2021

claim: The authors previously used TPP to measure changes to the T. gondii proteome when depleting the mitochondrial protein DegP2.
source: and to measure changes to the T. gondii proteome when depleting the mitochondrial protein DegP2 (Harding et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harding et al., 2020

claim: Intracellular free Ca2+ levels span three orders of magnitude, from low nanomolar in the cytoplasm to high micromolar in organelles like the ER.
source: Intracellular free Ca2+ levels span three orders of magnitude, from low nanomolar in the cytoplasm to high micromolar in organelles like the ER (Lourido and Moreno, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lourido and Moreno, 2015

claim: The conformational changes of TgCDPK1 have been structurally characterized.
source: As a proof of principle, we measured the thermal stability of the Ca2+-dependent protein kinase TgCDPK1, as the conformational changes of this enzyme have been structurally characterized (Ingram et al., 2015; Wernimont et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ingram et al., 2015 and Wernimont et al., 2010

claim: TgCDPK1 was strongly stabilized by Ca2+ as measured by immunoblot band intensity.
source: As measured by immunoblot band intensity, TgCDPK1 was strongly stabilized by Ca2+ (Figure 2A), suggesting that our experimental system is sensitive to Ca2+-dependent stability changes.
evidence: Data from immunoblot experiments with reference to Figure 2A

claim: The calculated EC50 of TgCDPK1 using the thermal profiling approach was in the low µM range.
source: The calculated EC50 using this approach was in the low µM range, consistent with studies using recombinant enzymes (Ingram et al., 2015; Wernimont et al., 2010).
evidence: Data from the thermal profiling experiments compared to literature values

claim: The study generated thermal profiles of the T. gondii proteome without or with 10 µM Ca2+.
source: Therefore, we first generated thermal profiles of the T. gondii proteome without or with 10 µM Ca2+, which is representative of the resting and stimulated Ca2+ concentrations of cell cytoplasm (Lourido and Moreno, 2015).
evidence: Description of experimental approach with citation to Lourido and Moreno, 2015

claim: The study detected 3,754 proteins in the thermal profiling experiments.
source: We detected 3,754 proteins, of which 2,381 yielded thermal profiles for both conditions in both replicates (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Data from the thermal profiling experiments with reference to figures

claim: 2,381 proteins yielded thermal profiles for both conditions in both replicates.
source: We detected 3,754 proteins, of which 2,381 yielded thermal profiles for both conditions in both replicates (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Data from the thermal profiling experiments with reference to figures

claim: The median melting temperatures were 54.4 and 54.7°C in the lysates without and with Ca2+, respectively.
source: The median melting temperatures—the temperatures at which proteins are 50% denatured—were 54.4 and 54.7°C in the lysates without and with Ca2+, respectively.
evidence: Data from the thermal profiling experiments

claim: The distribution of melting temperatures was largely overlapping in the two conditions.
source: The distribution of melting temperatures was largely overlapping in the two conditions (Figure 2D), suggesting that Ca2+-dependent changes in protein stability were restricted to a subset of proteins.
evidence: Data from the thermal profiling experiments with reference to Figure 2D

claim: Ca2+-dependent changes in protein stability were restricted to a subset of proteins.
source: The distribution of melting temperatures was largely overlapping in the two conditions (Figure 2D), suggesting that Ca2+-dependent changes in protein stability were restricted to a subset of proteins.
evidence: Inference from the distribution of melting temperatures

claim: The study identified parasite-specific proteins with EF hands as Ca2+-responsive, including TgCDPK7 and the calmodulin-like proteins CAM1 and CAM2.
source: Our analysis identified as Ca2+-responsive parasite-specific proteins with EF hands, including TgCDPK7 and the calmodulin-like proteins CAM1 and CAM2 (Table 1, Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Data from the thermal profiling experiments with references to table and figures

claim: Membrane proteins, including potential Ca2+-leak channels localizing to the ER, exhibited thermal shifts.
source: Membrane proteins, including potential Ca2+-leak channels localizing to the ER (Barylyuk et al., 2020; TGGT1_255900 and 206320), also exhibited thermal shifts (Figure 2F).
evidence: Data from the thermal profiling experiments with citation to Barylyuk et al., 2020 and reference to Figure 2F

claim: Several proteins specific to the apicomplexan parasite phylum exhibited Ca2+-regulation.
source: Several proteins specific to the apicomplexan parasite phylum exhibited Ca2+-regulation (Barylyuk et al., 2020; Sidik et al., 2016a), including an apical lysine methyltransferase (AKMT) that relocalizes during Ca2+-stimulated egress Heaslip et al., 2011; DrpC, which regulates the stability of parasite organelles; a hypothetical protein (TGGT1_214340) with no annotated domains (Figure 2—figure supplement 1); and enzyme subunits involved in cellular metabolism.
evidence: Data from the thermal profiling experiments with multiple citations and reference to figure

claim: A divergent subunit of the mitochondrial complex III, TgQCR9, was destabilized by Ca2+.
source: A divergent subunit of the mitochondrial complex III, TgQCR9, as well as components of the ATP synthase complex, were destabilized by Ca2+ (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Data from the thermal profiling experiments with reference to figure

claim: Components of the ATP synthase complex were destabilized by Ca2+.
source: A divergent subunit of the mitochondrial complex III, TgQCR9, as well as components of the ATP synthase complex, were destabilized by Ca2+ (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Data from the thermal profiling experiments with reference to figure

claim: The apicomplexan mitochondrion has been reported to sense cytosolic Ca2+ fluctuations.
source: The apicomplexan mitochondrion has been reported to sense cytosolic Ca2+ fluctuations (Gazarini and Garcia, 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Gazarini and Garcia, 2004

claim: The apicoplast may take up Ca2+ through direct contact sites with the ER.
source: and the apicoplast may take up Ca2+ through direct contact sites with the ER (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2021

claim: Redox signals were recently reported to induce parasite Ca2+ signaling and motility.
source: Furthermore, redox signals were recently reported to induce parasite Ca2+ signaling and motility (Alves et al., 2021; Stommel et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Alves et al., 2021 and Stommel et al., 1997

claim: All of the Ca2+-responsive ATP synthase elements protrude into the mitochondrial matrix.
source: The recent structure of the apicomplexan ATP synthase suggests that all of the Ca2+-responsive elements identified here, including subunits restricted to apicomplexan parasites, protrude into the mitochondrial matrix (Mühleip et al., 2021), which has elevated Ca2+ (Giorgi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mühleip et al., 2021 and Giorgi et al., 2018

claim: Plants and algae have Ca2+-sensing thioredoxins (calredoxins) in chloroplasts.

evidence: Supported by citations to Hochmal et al., 2016 and Charoenwattanasatien et al., 2020

claim: Clear responses were observed for several known Ca2+-binding enzymes with EF hands, including calmodulin, calcineurin, and several parasite Ca2+-dependent protein kinases (CDPKs).
source: Clear responses were observed for several known Ca2+-binding enzymes with EF hands, including calmodulin, calcineurin, and several parasite Ca2+-dependent protein kinases (CDPKs; Figure 3A).

claim: TgCDPK1, TgCDPK2A, and TgCDPK3 were stabilized by Ca2+.
source: These parameters can be used to classify proteins as stabilized (AUC >1; e.g., TgCDPK1, TgCDPK2A, and TgCDPK3) or destabilized (AUC <1; e.g., calmodulin and calcineurin B) by Ca2+ (Figure 3A).
evidence: Data from the concentration-range experiments with reference to Figure 3A

claim: Calmodulin and calcineurin B were destabilized by Ca2+.
source: These parameters can be used to classify proteins as stabilized (AUC >1; e.g., TgCDPK1, TgCDPK2A, and TgCDPK3) or destabilized (AUC <1; e.g., calmodulin and calcineurin B) by Ca2+ (Figure 3A).
evidence: Data from the concentration-range experiments with reference to Figure 3A

claim: Of the 4,403 proteins identified with sufficient quantification values for curve fitting, 228 were classified as Ca2+-responsive.
source: Of the 4,403 proteins identified with sufficient quantification values for curve fitting, 228 were classified as Ca2+-responsive based on exhibiting a dose-response trend (R2) greater than 0.8 with a stability change (AUC) of two modified Z scores from the median (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 2).

claim: Ca2+-responsive proteins were significantly enriched in Ca2+-binding functions, protein kinase activity, and metal affinity.
source: Functional enrichment showed that such Ca2+-responsive proteins were significantly enriched in Ca2+-binding functions, protein kinase activity, and metal affinity (Figure 3C).

claim: 25 of the 40 EF hand domain–containing proteins detected exhibited dose-responsive behavior.

claim: TgCDPK2A and CaM responded robustly with nM EC50.
source: Signaling and trafficking proteins were tuned to respond at lower Ca2+ concentrations: TgCDPK2A and CaM responded robustly with nM EC50
